title: Deleting B, searching for C
hook: C is still in the table. Will the search still find it?

knows: linear probing: a key whose slot is taken moves to the next free slot (probing-clusters-grow)
doesNotKnow: that emptying a slot can hide keys stored past it
that a delete leaves a marker saying keep looking

misconception: Deleting from a hash table just means emptying the key's slot.
objective: The learner can explain that a linear-probing search stops at an empty slot, so a delete must leave a gone marker or the keys stored past the gap become unreachable.

claims.text: In an 8-slot table where A, B, C all hash to slot 1 and sit in slots 1, 2, 3, emptying slot 2 and searching for C probes slot 1 (A) and slot 2 (empty), stops, and reports C not found.
claims.source: Builder's node run of linear-probing search (scratchpad algo10-verify.mjs): probes [1 A, 2 empty], stop, not found.

claims.text: With a gone marker in slot 2 instead, the same search probes slot 1 (A), slot 2 (gone), slot 3 (C) and finds C in slot 3.
claims.source: Builder's node run: probes [1 A, 2 gone, 3 C], found in slot 3.

claims.text: A linear-probing search treats an empty slot as the end of the run, so emptying B's slot breaks the search for every key stored past it.
claims.source: Search stops at the first empty slot (CLRS 4th ed. 11.4, open addressing search); a key stored past a slot that later became empty is never reached.

claims.text: Open-addressing deletion marks the slot with a special value (DELETED) instead of emptying it, so the search keeps looking past it.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. 11.4 (deleting from an open-addressing table by storing DELETED instead of NIL).

claims.text: Markers pile up and slow searches, so tables get rebuilt now and then.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. 11.4: with DELETED markers the search time no longer depends on the load factor alone, which is why chaining is more common when keys are deleted. Rebuilding is general practice, not a CLRS claim; fact-checker to confirm wording.

recall.question: A linear-probing table has keys X, Y, Z in slots 4, 5, 6, all hashed to 4. You delete Y by emptying slot 5, then search for Z. What happens?
options: The search stops at slot 5 and says Z is not there
The search finds Z in slot 6
recall.why: The search treats an empty slot as the end of the run. A gone marker in slot 5 would have told it to keep looking.

references.note: Open addressing: deletion with a DELETED marker
